en: The horse he rode beneath him,
Was Temir Khan's winged steed.
What he held in his hand for sport,
Was his father Ismayyl's falcon.
Down toward Bukhara, excited,
Flying his falcon in high spirits,
In the wake of his excitement,
In his passion for amusement,
He met his elder sister.
So many worries could not fit in her breast,
Then your elder sister Kanykey,
Her tears streamed in all directions.
That elder sister of yours, Kanykey,
Walked obliquely across his path,
Began words full of suffering,
Speaking softly, striking hard.
Each word she spoke
Ate away at the entrusted soul.
Speaking fitting words,
At that moment Kanykey,
The gray pouch-belt left by Manas,
Fitted it closely around her neck.
The poor woman stood wailing,
Pleading with Semetey.
“Little brother,” she began:
“My dear little brother,
Turn your horse's head and stop.
I shall tell much of my sorrow,
My noble younger brother, wait.
My white palace is what I lament.
I shall tell my grief, wait,
I shall lament at length.
I have a pit lying dug for me.
Turn back, younger brother, wait.
I have a calamity to tell you in lament.
We shall sell our coursers and pay tribute;
God has exhausted my strength.
From my fortunate Kyrgyz people,
Wandering, fleeing my homeland,
‘When a woman's husband dies,
Her birth-family is close,’ they say.
To this city of Bukhara,
I am a poor woman who fled.
Heed your poor elder sister.
Upon a woman such as me,
My royal younger brother, cast your eyes.
Little brother, when I lived in Talas,
Leaving no part of the earth untouched,
I went about pressing forward.
Over all the face of the earth,
I was a sovereign.
My blessed prosperity,
I had as much as any person.
Brother, I was left behind then,
Parted from my Blood-Drinker,
At thirty-two years of age.
In my youth I knew prosperity.
After your brother-in-law passed away,
I knew hardship to the full.
Whatever I grasped became embers.
Whatever I saw was a mass of arrows.
Where I lay became a deep hollow.
Sharing a father with me,
The six villains became accursed enemies.
Unable to cross Kuyuk Pass,
This became the occasion to save my life:
Burning with grief, unable to lie down and weep,
Unable to cross Jorgo Pass,
A time of great sorrow dawned.
I, your bereaved elder sister,
Grieving and weeping, unable to walk,
Unable to ford the Syr-Darya properly,
Unable to reach the place I longed for,
The soles of my feet all cut open,
Both feet torn to pieces,
Ruined, unable to take a stride,
My knees buckled when I stepped.
I, the frantic woman, cried and screamed,
Despairing of my precious life.
Unable to cross the hazy desert,
Unable to reach this Bukhara,
Running across the steppe,
Exhausted, despairing of life,
Unable to run across the ridge,
My orphaned soul suffered greatly.
When I came to Besh-Moynokcho,
Meeting me face to face,
Slaughtered for me by Bakay,
His pale two-year-old wether with a white blaze,
It will not leave my heart until I die,
What the six villains did in Talas.
My father Bakay, the leopard,
Came shouting up behind me.
He gave me two swift horses,
He gave me many skins of milk.
‘Flee to Bukhara,’ he said.
My father Bakay gave me strength.
He joined what had broken,
He gathered what had scattered.
He kindled my extinguished fire,
Revived a dying soul.
He camped with me on the steep slope,
Mighty Bakay, touched by Kydyr,
Helped me in my distress.
Turn your horse's head and wait,
My fortunate younger brother Semetey.
Stop on the ground ahead.
My white palace is what I lament.
Little brother, child, wait,
I shall tell much of my grief.
When I remember your brother-in-law,
Little brother, I grieve as though he had just died.
My father Temir Khan,
My sibling Ismayyl,
My great younger brother Semetey,
‘May all three of you live unharmed,’
Little brother, I keep asking God.
I hear news from those who come:
‘In this city of Bukhara,
The boy Semetey has newly
Become sovereign,’ I hear.
‘He has put on my golden crown,’
People from many lands say.
‘He has mounted the golden throne.
Here in this Bukhara,
He rules as governor,’ they say.
May your games be blessed!
May this feast of yours be full of strength.
May your coal become gold.
Oh, let me go before you,
May your life stretch far!
What is seen today is gone tomorrow.
I have seen the world's falsehood.
To hold and cherish,
From your brother-in-law gone to the other world,
No male child was left behind.
There is no spring flowing before me.
From your kingly, fierce brother-in-law,
No male light was left behind.
Nine multitudes of horses in the mountains,
Fine steeds and swift horses mixed,
Fine steeds, winged horses, have no brains.
The countless overflowing riches
Were left upon the steppe,
With no master to gather them.
We amassed six multitudes of thoroughbreds,
All dun, none piebald.
From your ocean, your fierce brother-in-law,
May I circle around you,
There is no boy like you.
The decree imposed by God,
There is no choice but to bear it.
What you desire today is gone tomorrow.
Such is the wretched ember.
Little brother, I was at ease, then withered and faded.
The Creator marked out this deed.
Little brother, I wandered and settled in Bukhara.
All the people around
Were made to call me ‘a wandering woman.’
I came to have a bad name.
Consider this matter, younger brother,
My forehead bone is curved back.
When your brother-in-law passed away,
There was not a speck of good fortune.
My means of living were scant.
For one who has fled here,
Bukhara is a good place.
The common people of Bukhara,
Who speak many impious words,
Have become so corrupt a people.
‘Into Temir Khan's city,
This one came wandering,
Settling with her household in Bukhara,
A shameless woman,’ they say.
Wandering to Bukhara,
I came and settled to save my life.
They have called me ‘a runaway woman.’
My dear little brother,
This year I have acquired a bad name.
If you heed me, little brother,
Come from time to time.
Ride over and call at the house.
Does a widow have no food?
Come and eat when you can.
Step across my threshold and come in.
Whatever robe my hands can make,
Regard it as a great gift,
And wear that robe of mine.
How your elder sister has suffered,
My dear little brother,
From now on, know it.
Come and sit in conversation.
A widow like me,
Keep asking how she fares.
Come to our home.
‘How are you faring?’ ask,
And cast your eyes upon me.
Little brother, when your valiant brother-in-law lived,
We too were khans like you.
Sending off people, receiving guests,
We were as good as anyone.
Your brother-in-law Manas was a hero.
One like your brother-in-law, the one God,
In creating a living mortal,
Will never create again.
That brother-in-law amassed the gold.
I, your elder sister, bore the suffering.
The six villains enjoyed its worth.
That brother-in-law amassed the silver.
This elder sister bore the grief.
The six villains enjoyed its benefit.
Little brother, my gold became like coal.
The forty champions left by your brother-in-law Manas,
Grown fat, they raided my settlement.
My silver turned to coal.
Sharing a father with your brother-in-law,
Those dogs of mine grew fat, knowing nothing of grief.
They ate my well-fed foal.
When they came spurring up,
Those base-born dogs of mine
Said, ‘I am an equal-born brother.’
My homespun silk became like felt.
They did not value me in the end.
My wealth became like felt.
After your brother-in-law passed away,
The six villains ruined my wealth in the end.
They brought violence and strife to my court.
They put the widow to such a test.
Raiding my migrating camp from Talas,
A curse upon being a woman,
With no male child left behind,
I left without taking revenge upon the dogs.
In Talas they slaughtered my Sart.
A curse upon widowhood,
Against the villain who rose in frenzy,
I could not take revenge.
My dear little brother,
Ride over and call at the house.
Come and sit in conversation.
‘How are things with you?’ ask.
Ask about my wretched life.
Set your horse's saddle right before you go.
For your brother-in-law gone to the other world,
Recite the Quran well before you go.
Step across the threshold and come in.
Your lamenting elder sister,
Learn how she lives and fares.”
Speaking these words then,
The beauty among the dusky-complexioned,
My dear elder sister Kanykey,
The radiant one among Muslims,
The youngest of twelve daughters,
God's beloved mortal,
My wretched elder sister Kanykey,
Who had been khan over all the people,
Had become thin.
